UDiscover: Gano's teenage discovery of bands like the Ramones and the Velvet Underground; Please Kill Me names the Velvets among the band's influences and calls Reed's influence on Gano's songwriting clear; a Gano biography traces garage-band covers moving through to Lou Reed and VU songs by 1979.
A Gano biography (wiki-scraper tier) lists Eno among what Gano's older NYC-based siblings exposed him to, alongside VU, Lou Reed, Patti Smith, Jonathan Richman, the B-52's.
UDiscover: the Femmes' acoustic approach was partly inspired by Jonathan Richman's Modern Lovers.
A Gano biography lists Patti Smith among what Gordon Gano's older NYC-based siblings exposed him to, alongside the Velvet Underground, Lou Reed, Jonathan Richman and the B-52's.

AllMusic's prose biography: "Intimate, experimental-leaning lo-fi pop from a Pennsylvania songwriter/guitarist who takes influence from Elliott Smith and Built to Spill."
The same AllMusic prose biography of Duster credits the band's patient, minimal approach as an influence on Alex G as well as Snail Mail.

Ben Ratliff, "A Stew of Rock and Pop Influences, Mixed Well and Served Slickly," The New York Times (9 Dec 2008), hearing the Breeders, Stereolab, krautrock and Sonic Youth's noise breakdowns in the live set -- the reviewer's reading, not the band's account.
AV Club: On Fire cast a wide shadow over Beach House, Deerhunter, Pains of Being Pure at Heart, Broken Social Scene.

Pitchfork's October 1999 review of Pinback's self-titled debut, by Andrew Goldman, wrote that "Pinback may be ready to join the ranks of emotionally confused super-songwriters alongside Modest Mouse, Sunny Day Real Estate, and the Sea and Cake."
Pitchfork's October 1999 review, grouping Pinback with Sunny Day Real Estate, Modest Mouse and the Sea and Cake as fellow "emotionally confused super-songwriters."
Spin's Garrett Kamps, reviewing Worlds, "identified melodic similarities with Boards of Canada."
A Salon review by Stephanie Zacharek traces threads in Sleater-Kinney's "Ironclad" back to Eddie Cochran and X-Ray Spex.
Stereogum: OTC's experimentalism audible in bigger bands including Radiohead, the Flaming Lips, Stereolab and the Shins. (Collective.)
Grammy.com's "Inside Elephant 6" feature, describing the collective rather than this band alone: it "has inspired acts like Arcade Fire, the Shins, and Tame Impala."

Grove Atlantic's publisher copy for the authorised GBV biography: P.J. Harvey, Radiohead, R.E.M., the Strokes and U2 have cited Pollard as an influence. Publisher marketing copy, not a primary interview.

Spin described the Strokes as "almost like the Ramones," and NME's "Roots Of" piece places the Ramones -- "the ultimate gang, beautifully ugly, masters of melodic dissonance" -- alongside the Velvet Underground and Talking Heads as the New York lineage the Strokes drew their sound and self-presentation from.
AllMusic's prose bio and NPR both describe the debt; no direct artist statement has surfaced.

Tim Sendra's AllMusic biography, describing the band's sound as an intermixture of "postmodern, Pavement-style pop" and the "loose, spacious jamming" of Neil Young -- a stylistic comparison rather than a stated influence.
A record-shop reissue write-up: the album has been influencing bands including Arcade Fire, Caribou and even Franz Ferdinand.
Spectrum Culture and Stereogum both name Bark Psychosis's "Absent Friend" as a blueprint for Explosions in the Sky's sound.
AllMusic bio: "Chiefly influenced by Kraftwerk and David Bowie's Berlin-era collaborations with Brian Eno"; Wikipedia notes Bowie/Eno's Low-era work informed Numan's 1981 album Dance.
Far Out: heavily influenced by contemporaries such as R.E.M.; Spin's 1995 album guide ties the post-lo-fi shift to touring with R.E.M.

Will Hodgkinson, "Interpol: misery loves a comeback," The Times (9 Jul 2022), on songs "recalling the post-punk iciness of Echo & the Bunnymen and Siouxsie and the Banshees" -- a critic's comparison, not a claim the band makes.

Rob Sheffield's Rolling Stone review of Turn On the Bright Lights (14 Aug 2002), drawing comparisons to Joy Division, Echo and the Bunnymen and the Smiths -- a critic's reading. Note the band has publicly denied the Joy Division comparison elsewhere.
Pitchfork's review of Census Designated (Kieran Press-Reynolds) compared her shift toward "a blend of shoegaze and bedroom pop" directly to My Bloody Valentine and Slowdive.

Stereogum (Ian Cohen), introducing a Q&A on her debut Frailty: her songs are "rooted just enough in familiar formats -- the saturated, EDM-adjacent ultrapop of Porter Robinson; SoundCloud rap's glitchy, bitcrushed production; the cleansing catharsis of emo."
